```{r}
#| include: false
# crit_plot(): z curve with the rejection region shaded, the critical value(s) as
# dashed red line(s), and the observed z as a solid blue line
crit_plot <- function(tail, z_obs, alpha = .05) {
  x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 400)
  par(mar = c(4, 1, 1, 1))
  plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "z", ylab = "", yaxt = "n",
       bty = "n", ylim = c(0, 0.47))
  shade <- function(a, b) {
    xs <- seq(a, b, length.out = 100)
    polygon(c(a, xs, b), c(0, dnorm(xs), 0), col = adjustcolor("firebrick", .4), border = NA)
  }
  cv <- switch(tail,
               lower = qnorm(alpha),
               upper = qnorm(1 - alpha),
               two   = c(qnorm(alpha / 2), qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)))
  if (tail == "lower") shade(-4, cv)
  if (tail == "upper") shade(cv, 4)
  if (tail == "two")   { shade(-4, cv[1]); shade(cv[2], 4) }
  abline(v = cv, col = "firebrick", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
  abline(v = z_obs, col = "#377EB8", lwd = 3)
  near <- cv[which.min(abs(cv - z_obs))]          # the cutoff on the same side
  outward <- abs(z_obs) > abs(near)               # is our z beyond that cutoff?
  # put each cutoff's label on the side away from our z line
  cpos <- ifelse(cv < 0, 2, 4)
  if (outward) cpos[cv == near] <- ifelse(near < 0, 4, 2)
  text(cv, 0.45, paste("critical z =", sprintf("%.3f", cv)), col = "firebrick", font = 2,
       cex = 1.1, pos = cpos)
  text(z_obs, 0.30, paste("our z =", z_obs), col = "#377EB8", font = 2, cex = 1.1,
       pos = ifelse(xor(z_obs < 0, !outward), 2, 4))
}
```

## Lab 7 Review: Lower-Tailed Test {style="font-size:78%"}

A sleep researcher predicts that GT students sleep **less** than the national average of $\mu$ = 7 hours ($\sigma$ = 1.2). A sample of $n$ = 36 GT students sleeps $\bar{x}$ = 6.6 hours. $\alpha$ = .05

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
$H_0$: $\mu \ge 7$ $H_1$: $\mu < 7$ → **lower tail**

All of $\alpha$ goes in the **left** tail:

```{r}
qnorm(.05)    # qnorm(alpha)
(6.6 - 7) / (1.2 / sqrt(36))
```

::: fragment
$z$ = −2.0 ≤ −1.645 → **reject** $H_0$: GT students sleep less than 7 hours
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
crit_plot("lower", z_obs = -2.0)
```
:::
:::::

## Lab 7 Review: Upper-Tailed Test {style="font-size:78%"}

A tutoring program claims it **raises** exam scores above the average of $\mu$ = 70 ($\sigma$ = 15). A sample of $n$ = 25 tutored students scores $\bar{x}$ = 76. $\alpha$ = .05

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
$H_0$: $\mu \le 70$ $H_1$: $\mu > 70$ → **upper tail**

All of $\alpha$ goes in the **right** tail:

```{r}
qnorm(1 - .05)    # qnorm(1 - alpha)
(76 - 70) / (15 / sqrt(25))
```

::: fragment
$z$ = 2.0 ≥ 1.645 → **reject** $H_0$: tutoring raises exam scores
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
crit_plot("upper", z_obs = 2.0)
```
:::
:::::

## Lab 7 Review: Two-Tailed Test, $\bar{x}$ > $\mu$ {style="font-size:78%"}

Does caffeine **change** reaction time? Population: $\mu$ = 250 ms, $\sigma$ = 40. A sample of $n$ = 64 people who drank coffee averages $\bar{x}$ = 262 ms. $\alpha$ = .05

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
$H_0$: $\mu = 250$ $H_1$: $\mu \ne 250$ → **two tails**, $\alpha$/2 = .025 in each

$\bar{x}$ is **above** $\mu$, so compare with the **upper** cutoff:

```{r}
qnorm(1 - .05 / 2)    # qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
(262 - 250) / (40 / sqrt(64))
```

::: fragment
$z$ = 2.4 ≥ 1.96 → **reject** $H_0$: caffeine changes reaction time
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
crit_plot("two", z_obs = 2.4)
```
:::
:::::

## Lab 7 Review: Two-Tailed Test, $\bar{x}$ < $\mu$ {style="font-size:78%"}

Does a new font **change** reading speed? Population: $\mu$ = 200 words per minute, $\sigma$ = 30. A sample of $n$ = 36 readers using the new font averages $\bar{x}$ = 191. $\alpha$ = .05

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
$H_0$: $\mu = 200$ $H_1$: $\mu \ne 200$ → **two tails**, $\alpha$/2 = .025 in each

$\bar{x}$ is **below** $\mu$, so compare with the **lower** cutoff:

```{r}
qnorm(.05 / 2)    # qnorm(alpha/2)
(191 - 200) / (30 / sqrt(36))
```

::: fragment
$z$ = −1.8 is **not** beyond −1.96 → **fail to reject** $H_0$: no evidence the font changes reading speed
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
crit_plot("two", z_obs = -1.8)
```
:::
:::::

# Confidence Intervals {.center}

## What Is a Confidence Interval? {style="font-size:85%"}

A **confidence interval (CI)** is a range of plausible values for the population mean $\mu$, built around our sample mean

::: subpoint
○ A 95% CI: if we repeated the study many times, **95% of the intervals** built this way would contain $\mu$
:::

::: subpoint
○ It uses the same $z$ cutoffs you already know
:::

| Confidence level | $\alpha$ | $z$ cutoffs |       R       |
|:----------------:|:--------:|:-----------:|:-------------:|
|       68%        |   .32    |     ±1      | `qnorm(.84)`  |
|       95%        |   .05    |    ±1.96    | `qnorm(.975)` |
|       99%        |   .01    |    ±2.58    | `qnorm(.995)` |

::: fragment
Confidence level = $1 - \alpha$. Each tail gets $\alpha / 2$, so the cutoff is `qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)`
:::

## Confidence Level and Width {style="font-size:85%"}

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="45%"}
```{webr}
qnorm(1 - .05 / 2)    # 95% CI
qnorm(1 - .027 / 2)   # 97.3% CI
```

::: fragment
Which interval is wider?

**97.3%**: to be **more confident** we catch $\mu$, we need a **wider** net
:::
::::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.8
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 400)
par(mar = c(4, 1, 1, 1))
plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "z", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", ylim = c(0, 0.5))
arrows(-1.96, 0.44, 1.96, 0.44, code = 3, angle = 90, length = .05, lwd = 3, col = "#377EB8")
arrows(-2.21, 0.48, 2.21, 0.48, code = 3, angle = 90, length = .05, lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
text(0, 0.44, "95%: ±1.96", pos = 1, col = "#377EB8", font = 2)
text(2.4, 0.48, "97.3%: ±2.21", pos = 4, col = "firebrick", font = 2, xpd = TRUE)
```
:::
::::::

## The CI Formula {style="font-size:85%"}

$$\text{CI} = \bar{x} \pm z^{*} \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

::: subpoint
○ $\bar{x}$: the sample mean, the center of the interval
:::

::: subpoint
○ $z^{*}$: the cutoff for our confidence level (1.96 for 95%)
:::

::: subpoint
○ $s / \sqrt{n}$: the standard error
:::

:::: fragment
**Lower bound** $= \bar{x} - z^{*} \times SE$ **Upper bound** $= \bar{x} + z^{*} \times SE$

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
ⓘ Why the minus? The lower cutoff is $-1.96$, so $\bar{x} + (-1.96) \times SE$ is the same as $\bar{x} - 1.96 \times SE$
:::
::::

## CI Example: Iris Petal Length {style="font-size:85%"}

95% CI for the mean petal length of iris flowers (built-in `iris` data)

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{webr}
#| autorun: true
x_bar  <- mean(iris$Petal.Length)
s      <- sd(iris$Petal.Length)
n      <- length(iris$Petal.Length)
se     <- s / sqrt(n)
z_star <- qnorm(.975)

c(lower = x_bar - z_star * se,
  upper = x_bar + z_star * se)
```
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="40%"}
We are 95% confident that the mean petal length of irises is between **3.48** and **4.04** cm
:::
:::::

## What Does "95% Confident" Mean? {style="font-size:80%"}

Simulate 100 studies from a population with $\mu$ = 100, $\sigma$ = 15, and build a 95% CI in each

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
set.seed(2020)
lower <- upper <- rep(NA, 100)
for (i in 1:100) {
  x  <- rnorm(25, mean = 100, sd = 15)
  se <- 15 / sqrt(25)
  lower[i] <- mean(x) - qnorm(.975) * se
  upper[i] <- mean(x) + qnorm(.975) * se
}
hit <- lower <= 100 & upper >= 100
mean(hit)   # proportion of CIs that caught mu

plot(NA, xlim = range(lower, upper), ylim = c(1, 100),
     xlab = "", ylab = "study")
segments(lower, 1:100, upper, 1:100, lwd = 2,
         col = ifelse(hit, "grey60", "firebrick"))
abline(v = 100, lwd = 2, col = "#377EB8")
```
:::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
Each line is one study's CI. The blue line is the true $\mu$

::: fragment
About 95 of 100 intervals catch $\mu$; the red ones miss

The 95% describes the **method**, not any one interval
:::
::::
::::::

## CIs and NHST {style="font-size:85%"}

A 95% CI and a two-tailed test with $\alpha$ = .05 always agree:

::: subpoint
○ The CI **excludes** $\mu_0$ → **reject** $H_0$ ($p$ \< .05)
:::

::: subpoint
○ The CI **includes** $\mu_0$ → **fail to reject** $H_0$
:::

::: fragment
Example: someone claims the mean petal length is $\mu_0$ = 3.3 cm

Our 95% CI is \[3.48, 4.04\]. Is 3.3 inside?
:::

::: fragment
No → **reject** $H_0$: the mean petal length differs from 3.3 cm
:::

# From *z* to *t*: the One-Sample *t*-Test {.center}

## *z*- vs. *t*-Distribution {style="font-size:85%"}

When we **don't know** $\sigma$ (almost always!), we estimate it with $s$ and use the ***t*****-distribution**

::: subpoint
○ Bell-shaped and symmetric, but with **thicker tails**
:::

::: subpoint
○ Its shape depends on the **degrees of freedom**: $df = n - 1$
:::

::: subpoint
○ As $df$ increases, it looks more and more like the standard normal ($z$) distribution
:::

::: subpoint
○ With $df = \infty$, it is exactly the normal distribution, so with a large $df$, $t \approx z$
:::

## *z*- vs. *t*-Distribution

```{r}
#| include: false
# plot_zt(k): standard normal plus the first k t-curves (df = 1, 2, 10, 100)
plot_zt <- function(k = 0) {
  x <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 1000)
  dfs  <- c(1, 2, 10, 100)
  cols <- c("#87C5E6", "#4A7FB5", "#335C8C", "#1E2A6E")
  labx <- c(-1.6, -1.25, -0.95, -0.45)
  par(mar = c(3, 2, 0.5, 2))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(-5, 5), ylim = c(0, 0.41), xlab = "", ylab = "",
       yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", bty = "n", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  axis(1, at = seq(-5, 5, 2.5), labels = format(seq(-5, 5, 2.5), nsmall = 1),
       lwd = 2, cex.axis = 1.3)
  # draw a curve with its label written along it
  curve_lab <- function(f, lx, lab, col, cex = 1.4) {
    y <- f(x)
    asp <- (par("pin")[2] / diff(par("usr")[3:4])) / (par("pin")[1] / diff(par("usr")[1:2]))
    slope <- (f(lx + 1e-4) - f(lx - 1e-4)) / 2e-4
    ang <- atan(slope * asp) * 180 / pi
    # leave a gap in the line where the label sits (distance measured in inches)
    sx <- par("pin")[1] / diff(par("usr")[1:2]); sy <- par("pin")[2] / diff(par("usr")[3:4])
    w  <- strwidth(lab, units = "inches", cex = cex) / 2 * 1.08
    y[sqrt(((x - lx) * sx)^2 + ((y - f(lx)) * sy)^2) < w] <- NA
    lines(x, y, lwd = 4, col = col)
    text(lx, f(lx), lab, srt = ang, col = col, cex = cex)
  }
  lines(x, dnorm(x), lwd = 4, col = "grey55")
  text(0.45, 0.395, "standard normal", pos = 4, col = "grey55", cex = 1.4)
  if (k > 0) for (i in 1:k)
    curve_lab(function(z) dt(z, dfs[i]), labx[i], paste0("t(df=", dfs[i], ")"), cols[i])
}
```

::: r-stack
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.2
plot_zt(0)
```

::: fragment

#| fig-height: 5.2

## Critical Values: `qt()` vs. `qnorm()` {style="font-size:85%"}

`qt()` works like `qnorm()`, but also needs the degrees of freedom

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{webr}
qnorm(.975)          # z cutoff, 95%
qt(.975, df = 5)     # n = 6
qt(.975, df = 30)    # n = 31
qt(.975, df = 233)   # n = 234
```
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="45%"}
Thicker tails → a **bigger** cutoff with small samples

With large samples, the $t$ cutoff is almost 1.96

`pt()` is the $t$ version of `pnorm()`
:::
:::::

## The One-Sample *t*-Test {style="font-size:85%"}

Same idea as the $z$-test, but with $s$ in place of $\sigma$:

$$t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}}, \qquad df = n - 1$$

R does every step for us with `t.test()`:

``` r
t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: subpoint
○ `x`: the sample data
:::

::: subpoint
○ `mu`: the population mean under $H_0$ (default 0)
:::

::: subpoint
○ `alternative`: `"two.sided"` (default), `"less"`, or `"greater"`
:::

## `t.test()` Example: Highway MPG {style="font-size:80%"}

A researcher claims cars average **30** highway mpg. Test it with the 234 cars in `mpg$hwy` (we don't know $\sigma$). One- or two-tailed?

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{webr}
#| autorun: true
result <- t.test(mpg$hwy, mu = 30)
result
```
:::

::::: {.column width="42%"}
::: fragment
Two-tailed: the claim gives no direction

$t$(233) = −16.85, $p$ \< .001 → **reject** $H_0$
:::

::: fragment
Pull out pieces with `$`:

``` r
result$statistic
result$p.value
result$conf.int
```

The 95% CI \[22.67, 24.21\] excludes 30, so the CI tells the same story
:::
:::::
:::::::

## One-Tailed `t.test()` {style="font-size:85%"}

What if the researcher had predicted, **before** looking, that cars get **less** than 30 mpg?

:::::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{webr}
t.test(mpg$hwy, mu = 30, alternative = "less")
```
:::

:::::: {.column width="45%"}
::: subpoint
○ `"less"` → $H_1$: $\mu$ \< 30 (lower tail)
:::

::: subpoint
○ `"greater"` → $H_1$: $\mu$ \> 30 (upper tail)
:::

::: fragment
The one-tailed $p$ is half the two-tailed $p$, and the CI becomes one-sided: (−Inf, 24.08\]
:::
::::::
::::::::

# Effect Size: Cohen's *d* {.center}

## Statistical vs. Practical Significance {style="font-size:85%"}

::: subpoint
○ **Statistical** significance: is there *any* difference?
:::

::: subpoint
○ **Practical** significance: how *big* is the difference?
:::

With a big enough $n$, even a tiny difference is significant, so we also report an **effect size**: the size of the effect, independent of sample size

$$d = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s}$$

| $|d|$ | Effect size |
|:-----:|:-----------:|
|  0.2  |    Small    |
|  0.5  |   Medium    |
|  0.8  |    Large    |

::: {style="font-size:70%"}
ⓘ Unlike $t$, there is no $\sqrt{n}$: we divide by the SD, not the standard error. Cohen's *d* is a description, not a test
:::

## Cohen's *d* in R: Highway MPG {style="font-size:85%"}

:::::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
```{webr}
#| autorun: true
d <- (mean(mpg$hwy) - 30) / sd(mpg$hwy)
d
```

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
ⓘ R's built-in Cohen's *d* functions are mostly for comparing two groups, so we compute the one-sample *d* by hand
:::
::::

::::::: {.column width="45%"}
::: fragment
$d$ = −1.10: a **large** effect. Cars average about 1.1 SDs **below** the claimed 30 mpg
:::

::::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%"}
True or false?

::: subpoint
○ Increasing the sample size increases the effect size: **False**
:::

::: subpoint
○ A larger difference between $\bar{x}$ and $\mu$ increases the effect size: **True** (it is the numerator)
:::
:::::
:::::::
::::::::::

Someone claims cars average **17** mpg in the city. Use `mpg$cty` ($\alpha$ = .05, two-tailed)

```{webr}
# a. run t.test() and report t, df, and p

# b. does the 95% CI include 17?

# c. Cohen's d

```

::: fragment
Check: $t$(233) = −0.51, $p$ = .61 → **fail to reject** $H_0$; the CI \[16.31, 17.41\] includes 17; $d$ = −0.03, a negligible effect
:::

## Must-Take-Home Message {style="font-size:90%"}

::: subpoint
○ A CI = $\bar{x} \pm$ cutoff × SE. Higher confidence → wider interval
:::

::: subpoint
○ A 95% CI that excludes $\mu_0$ ↔ reject $H_0$ in a two-tailed test at $\alpha$ = .05
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\sigma$ unknown → use $s$ and the $t$-distribution ($df = n - 1$); `qt()` for cutoffs, `t.test()` for the whole test
:::

::: subpoint
○ Significance asks *is there an effect?*; Cohen's $d = (\bar{x} - \mu) / s$ asks *how big?* (.2 small, .5 medium, .8 large)
:::
